ground_truth.title: The Ultimate Wedding-Planning Checklist and Timeline
ground_truth.author: Ellen O'Brien
ground_truth.main_content:
After announcing your engagement, you may be eager to jump into wedding planning—or feel incredibly overwhelmed by it all. Even if you’re not currently experiencing any stress related to your upcoming nuptials, there are so many details to consider when it comes to your big day—and the events leading up to it. Ultimately, it can be challenging for even the most organized brides and grooms to stay on top of all that needs to be done prior to walking down the aisle. However, know that by starting this process early, you’ll make it straightforward, fun—and much less anxiety-inducing. \”By breaking down the year month by month, you are taking on the planning process in bite-size pieces,\” says Tessa Lyn Brand, the founder of Tessa Lyn Events, a wedding-planning agency. \”You can enjoy each step.\”

While 12 to 14 months is the ideal length for an engagement, every couple’s timeline is different. For example, if you’re hoping to tie the knot in less than a year, know that you’ll likely need to condense your schedule. \”If you’re getting married in six months, try to complete all the wedding-planning checklist tasks designated for month 12 to six in that very first month, and then you’ll be right on schedule with everything else,\” Brand says.

Below, we created a 12-month wedding-planning checklist and timeline to help you stay on task in the weeks leading up to your big day. From when to book a key vendor to what month to schedule your final dress fitting for, this breakdown includes everything you need to know. Read on for more.

12 Months Out

Insure Your Engagement Ring

While this is technically something you’ll do prior to starting the wedding-planning process, it deserves special mention. If your partner didn’t purchase insurance when they bought the ring, make sure to do so as soon as possible.

Determine Your Budget

Before you can start anything, you and your partner need to determine who will be paying for your celebration—and how much you can spend. From there, you’ll start to figure out what aspects are and are not a priority. (A little market research here comes in handy.) Since these numbers will likely change as you begin to plan, start tracking everything on a detailed spreadsheet. This will help you know exactly what you’re spending and make it easy to adjust your numbers as needed.

Make a Guest List

Unfortunately, you likely can’t invite everyone you want to your nuptials. When deciding your headcount, consider your budget (how many guests can you really afford to host?) and your venue (how many people does it fit?). From there, you can start to divide up the guest list. If you and your partner are footing the bill, assume that you’ll get 70 percent of the invites while both sets of parents will split the other 30 percent. However, if your family is contributing toward the cost of the celebration, tradition dictates that all involved parties get one-third of the list to dedicated to their preferred attendees. Yet, if this doesn’t seem feasible to you, know that modern couples opt set their own standard for managing the guest list.

Hire a Wedding Planner

Again, this will depend on your budget (fair warning: most everything will), but if your funds allow, now is the time to hire the manager of your big day. A wedding planner will be your right-hand person throughout the process, guiding you in all decisions—from selecting a venue to booking vendors.

Decide Formality and Overall Theme

It’s time for another important conversation with your significant other. When determining what you want your celebration to feel and look like, ask yourselves: What’s important to us and why? What do we value? Also, know that your venue will likely affect this.

Select the Venue

Choosing the venue is one of the most important decisions you’ll make at the start of the planning process. The location affects almost everything else, from how many people you invite to what kind of flowers go on the table. It’s also likely one of your biggest expenses. Make sure to explore your options, make multiple site visits, and ultimately select a spot that fits your guest count, style, and budget.

Buy Wedding Insurance

Throwing a wedding is a major financial investment, so err on the side of prudence and purchase special events insurance to protect yourself from damage and liabilities on the big day. You can apply for coverage as soon as you start planning—or once you have your venue secured.

Select the Caterer

Your wedding is the best (and largest) dinner party of your life, which can often feel like an overwhelming feat. Start by hiring people you trust to deliver—whether that’s the venue’s in-house caterer, a team recommended by your planner, or even your favorite taco truck. And don’t be afraid to get creative with the menu. Guests will enjoy tasting your favorite cocktail just as much as Grandma’s famous blueberry pie.

11 Months Out

Choose a Color Palette and Start Thinking of Your Overall Design

It’s finally time to gather inspiration, select a color palette, and create a mood board. There are so many ideas out there, so take your time with this part of the process. Remember: It’s also okay to take a step back if you feel overwhelmed.

Hire Vendors Who Book Up Quickly, Including Your Photographer, Band, DJ, and Videographer

These are the people who will make your night fun—and capture the memories last forever. Do your research before you hire these key vendors, ask the right questions, and maybe even test your photographer out by having them take your engagement portraits.

10 Months Out

Start Shopping for Your Wedding Dress

It’s time to shop for your wedding dress. Stuck on where to shop for this all-important gown? Consider heading to a BRIDES Top Tier Salon. These editor-approved retailers will have the selection and service you need when making this critical purchase.

Book Hotel Room Blocks for Guests

It’s a thoughtful gesture to block out rooms (and secure a discounted rate) for your guests. Before you create a room block at random, check out our comprehensive guide on the subject to ensure your family and friends have the right accommodations.

Create Your Wedding Website

Start creating your wedding website now, as you’ll likely need to put the URL on your save-the-dates next month. Make sure to include key details, such as how to RSVP, where to stay, what to wear, and a link to your registry.

Take Engagement Photos

If you want to have engagement photos for your wedding website, save-the-dates, or general memories, now is the perfect time to take them. Pro tip: Some photographers may even include engagement photos in your wedding package.

Start Looking at Invitations

Your wedding invitation is a guest’s first impression of your big day. If you’re going custom, start working with a graphic designer or stationer now to create your dream suite. However, if you’re going for a less time-intensive route, you can wait until the six-month mark. (Invites will be sent out six to eight weeks before the big day.)

9 Months Out

Buy Your Wedding Dress

It’s time to say \”yes\” to the dress if you want to avoid rush fees. If you can place your order even earlier, that’s preferable.

Send Save-the-Dates

Let everyone officially know when and where you’re tying the knot. And remember: Everyone who gets a save-the-date gets a wedding invite.

8 Months Out

Register for Gifts

When registering for gifts, think about what you really want. Are you adventurers? Aspiring chefs? Constant travelers? Consider your hobbies and tailor the registry to your soon-to-be-married lifestyle.

Select Your Wedding-Party Attire

After purchasing your own gown, you’ll want to select the pieces for your wedding party. Regardless of whether you want them to wear mismatched dresses or appear in the same hue, make sure to give your loved ones plenty of time to order the correct ensemble.

Meet With Potential Florists

To find the right florist, consider asking friends for recommendations, scrolling through Instagram inspiration, and asking your wedding planner or venue coordinator who they may turn to for your vision. It’s important that you find someone who is able to deliver on your aesthetic—and budget.

7 Months Out

Book the Rehearsal-Dinner Venue

Traditionally, the groom’s family pays for the rehearsal dinner. With that said, some modern couples opt to foot the bill themselves or turn to other loved ones for financial support with this pre-nuptial celebration. Regardless of who’s organizing the event, make sure to touch base with them regarding key details.

Hire the Ceremony Musicians

If you’re hoping to enlist the talents of a three-piece band, now’s the time to make it official. Even if you’d just like a guitar or cello player for your processional, make sure to reserve them well in advance of your ceremony.

Order Rental Items

While rentals, such as chair, linens, and chargers, can often be an afterthought, they shouldn’t be: Great rentals essentially act as the bones of your wedding-day décor. Don’t skimp on upgraded chairs and cozy lounge furniture (your guests will thank you) if your budget allows for it.

Hire an Officiant

If you aren’t marrying in a house of worship, you’ll need to hire someone to make it official. Turn to a professional or take a more intimate approach and ask a close friend or family member to do the honors.

6 Months Out

Hire a Lighting Technician

Couples often forget about the lighting, but it’s an important detail you won’t want to miss. The bulbs and candles you select will ultimately be responsible for illuminating your venue, making your photos just right, and sustaining your party going—even after the sun sets.

5 Months Out

Book Transportation for Guests, If Needed

To know whether or not you need transportation, consider your venue’s parking situation, guests’ access to car services or public transportation, and the cost you’re asking them to incur. A good rule of thumb: If it’s going to run them $20 or more—especially if you’ve already asked them to travel for a destination wedding—consider a shuttle bus. Some car services, such as Uber, allow you to book rides on others’ behalf.

Book Your Transportation (Like a Limo or Specialty Car)

After you consider your guests, it’s time to think about you and your partner. Whether you want a stretch Escalade limo or a tandem bicycle, make sure to book it now.

Book the Honeymoon

Traditionally, wedding etiquette states the groom plans a surprise honeymoon for the bride, but if you’re tag-teaming the honeymoon strategy, try to have things semi-sorted out by the five-month mark. That means being on the same page about budget, timing, travel arrangements, and a rough itinerary.

Buy or Rent the Groom’s Tuxedo

You can opt to buy or rent your suit or tuxedo. When selecting the actual ensemble, focus on fit and function. A well-made outfit will be flattering, but it should also allow you to move freely.

Begin Premarital Counseling

Many couples attribute the success of their relationship to premarital counseling. An objective third party can help you address issues that emerge in your dynamic—and provide counselors healthy conflict-resolution tactics, so you’ll be ready when an inevitable disagreement does present itself.

Some states offer a discount on your marriage license if you undergo counseling.

4 Months Out

Have Your Final Tasting With the Caterer

After numerous conversations with your caterer, it’s time to taste the proposed menu. The tasting has become increasingly important as more and more couples choose to customize everythin—from their signature cocktails to their desserts. Consider bringing your planner to the meeting; they’ve likely attended dozens of tastings and will be your clear-eyed troubleshooter, paying attention to the detailing of the food and the attentiveness of the service.

Choose Your Cake

If you decide to have a wedding cake, this is the time to settle on a look and flavor profile. Instead of stressing out about pleasing every one of your guests, focus on the confection that would make you happy. When you know what you want, find a reputable baker who’s available on your date, and happy to take on your dream design at the right price point.

Buy Wedding Bands

Even though you received your engagement ring months ago, it’s time to shop for your and your partner’s wedding bands. Make sure to also purchase insurance for your new valuables.

Select the Groomsmen Attire and Schedule Fittings Within the Month

If you’re having groomsmen at your ceremony, this is the time to ensure they have their ensembles prepared. Send them a link on what to order—or make sure they know your preferred color scheme before they purchase an outfit.

Have Your Hair and Makeup Trial

Before heading to your hair and makeup trial, look back at old photos of yourself or social media posts of others for inspiration. Bring the pictures with you—and be as specific as possible with the stylist about what you do and don’t want.

3 Months Out

Order the Invitations and Hire a Calligrapher

There are a few ground rules when it comes to ordering wedding invitations: Order enough of them to account for some mistakes, make sure they’re able arrive in time, set up a system to record RSVP replies, and confirm all addresses and spelling. However, know that when it comes to the design and wording, the options are endless. Need a little advice to rein it all in? Remind yourself that the theme of your invites should match the vibe of the wedding and you as a couple.

Create or Plan Your Menu

Once you’ve undergone a successful tasting, you’ll have a good sense of a caterer’s style and offerings, so you’re ready to finalize the food. Maybe you hand-selected every hors d’oeuvre, main, side, dessert, and drink. Or, perhaps you just told the chef to \”handle it\” and called it a day. Either way, now is the time to stamp your approval on a completed menu that fits your budget, taste, and timing.

Brainstorm Guest Favors and Gift Bags

Favors and gift bags are option. However, if you want to do them, now is the time to decide what they will be. Stuck on endless options? Consider an edible treat, like bags of candy or a cookie.

Book a Photo-Booth Rental

Photo booths have become a reception staple. If you’re hoping for something with a little more pizzazz than the standard step-and-shoot, consider these creative alternatives.

Write Your Vows

If you’ve opted to write your own promises to one another, start thinking about what those should sound like for you two as a couple, whether that be traditional and classic or modern and innovative.

Select Readings

Bible verses are often an obvious choice here, but there are plenty of nonreligious options, too. If you’d prefer for designated readers to choose their own, make sure to give them as much guidance as possible.

Meet With Your Officiant

When considering an officiant, think about availability, eligibility, fee, and fit. Can your officiant of choice lawfully, affordably, and meaningfully help you two become one? Make sure they are on the same page as you about expectations and the overall tone of the ceremony. And if you’ve recruited a recently-ordained friend or family member to head up the charge, here’s an article on how to officiate a wedding ceremony to share with them.

Start Crafting DIY Items If You Haven’t Already

If you have any décor projects to tackle, it’s time to start crafting. Make sure to give yourself plenty of time to allow your vision to come to life.

2 Months Out

Send Out the Wedding Invitations (With RSVPs Due One Month Before the Wedding)

You already did the hard part—the selection process. Now, it’s time to print and assemble your invites. Be sure to include a self-addressed, pre-stamped envelope for your RSVP cards.

Send Out Rehearsal-Dinner Invitations

If your partner and their family are handling the rehearsal dinner, make sure you give them an accurate list of addresses for the invitees. You don’t want it to be an exact replica of the reception that will follow the next night, but you may also want to confirm you don’t show up to a BBQ buffet in black-tie. You can also opt to send these out with your formal invitations.

Have Your First Wedding Dress Fitting

Your first wedding dress fitting should occur two to three months after ordering your gown. Your second fitting should happen about six weeks before the big day.

Purchase Wedding Dress Undergarments

After your first dress fitting, it’s time to purchase the necessary undergarments. It’s best to wait until this point, as your first fitting will clarify what type of underpinnings—from shapewear to lingerie—the piece will require.

Pick Up Your Marriage License

It’s a crucial step that you don’t want to forget: getting your marriage license. Every state has different laws and requirements, so make sure to check for yours ahead of time. If you’re having a destination wedding, whether domestic or international, you’ll also need to research those paperwork requirements. Then, make sure you as a couple, your witness(es), and your officiant sign the document.

Buy Gifts for Your Wedding Party

How much you spend on gifts for your wedding party is ultimately up to you. However, no matter the price point, focus on gifting something thoughtful, functional, and personalized.

Do a Floral Mock-Up With Your Florist

Floral samples vary depending on the florist and your décor choices. However, typically, they’ll include a mock reception table setup, centerpiece, and bouquet. Make sure to flag any necessary tweaks and finalize your delivery and care strategy.

Give the Song Selections to Your Musicians

Now is the time to tell your band, DJ, or musicians what you want to hear at your wedding. If you need suggestions, start by considering the most popular wedding songs of all time, then think about tunes you and your soon-to-be spouse love.

Buy All Necessary Small Items

There are a number of small items you’ll want to secure before your wedding weekend, including table numbers, toasting flutes, a cake topper, a cake stand, a cake knife, the guest book, a card box, ring-bearer accessories and flower-girl accessories. You also may consider purchasing pashminas, flip-flops, and/or sunglasses for guests to change into at the reception, as well as baskets to hold them. And don’t forget your signs (\”Welcome,\” \”Guest Book,\” \”Dancing Shoes,\” etc.).

1 Month Out

Assemble Gift Bags

Follow the same guidelines as you did for for your DIY projects to ensure this task is fun rather than frustrating. Give yourself plenty of time to complete this to-do—and consider enlisting your friends for help.

Pay Vendors in Full

The last situation you want to deal with right before your wedding day is a vendor chasing their payment. Avoid that by keeping careful track of when and how much you pay each vendor. If there are some vendors who must be paid on the day of your wedding, or you’re distributing tips, delegate that role to a trusted friend or relative.

Create a Seating Chart

Creating the seating chart can feel like another daunting task. When completing this must-do, think about your venue’s floor plan, whether or not you’ll have a head table and who will be sitting at it, and your preferred design.

Order or Make Escort Cards and Place Cards

While both place cards and escort cards designate where each guest will be seated at a wedding, the former are more specific and formal than the latter. A place card not only directs guests to the table where they will sit during the reception, but also points them to their particular seat at the table. Whichever you choose, you’ll want the cards to complement your overall wedding theme.

Have a Final Venue Walk-Through

Make a list of questions beforehand, and take your planner or another close friend or family member to bring up anything you may forget.

Put Cash in Tip Envelopes for Your Planner/Delegate to Distribute

While you don’t need to tip people who own their own businesses, such as photographers, videographers, and florists, it’s typically customary to tip some vendors, including musicians, DJs, hair stylists, makeup artists, drivers, bartenders, and servers. Some couples also opt to tip their wedding planner.

Break in Your Wedding Shoes

Strut down your hallway. Dance in the kitchen. Do everything in your power to avoid painful blisters on your wedding night.

Final Week

Congratulations! You’ve made it all the way to the final week of wedding planning. Deep breaths now, most of the hard work is over at this point. Now’s the time to take care of the little things like:

- Manicure/pedicure
- Getting a massage
- Final dress fitting
- Pack your bags for the honeymoon (if you’re leaving after your wedding)
- Clean your ring
- Chase any RSVP stragglers and deliver the final headcount
- Clear your work to-do list so you can only focus on wedding festivities and take it all in
- Practice your vows out loud
- Write your partner a note

Night Before and Morning of the Wedding

The big day is finally here. All that careful preparation and creative planning have come to fruition, and it’s time to enjoy the wedding. Here’s what to do:

The Night Before:

- Eat a healthy meal
- Pack a clutch or small bag of personal items
- Drink water
- Get a good night’s sleep
- Put any boxes, suitcases, bags, and survival kits to bring to the ceremony or reception in the car

The Morning Of:

- Stay off your feet as much as possible
- Eat breakfast
- Drink even more water
- Take your dress and veil out of the bag early on and have someone steam them if needed
- Lay out all the items (rings, invitations, etc.) that you want the photographer to capture
- Exchange notes with your partner
- Say thank you to everyone around you

Regardless of who’s organizing the event, make sure to touch base with them regarding key details.

### Hire the Ceremony Musicians

If you’re hoping to enlist the talents of a three-piece band, now’s the time to make it official. Even if you’d just like a guitar or cello player for your processional, make sure to reserve them well in advance of your ceremony.

### Order Rental Items

While rentals, such as chair, linens, and chargers, can often be an afterthought, they shouldn’t be: Great rentals essentially act as the bones of your wedding-day décor. Don’t skimp on upgraded chairs and cozy lounge furniture (your guests will thank you) if your budget allows for it.

### Hire an Officiant

If you aren’t marrying in a house of worship, you’ll need [to hire someone to make it official](https://www.brides.com/how-to-find-and-choose-your-wedding-officiant-5224142). Turn to a professional or take a more intimate approach and ask a close friend or family member to do the honors.

## 6 Months Out

### Hire a Lighting Technician

Couples often forget about [the lighting](https://www.brides.com/wedding-lamp-ideas-8772242), but it’s an important detail you won’t want to miss. The bulbs and candles you select will ultimately be responsible for illuminating your venue, making your photos just right, and sustaining your party going—even after the sun sets.

## 5 Months Out

### Book Transportation for Guests, If Needed

To know whether or not you [need transportation](https://www.brides.com/story/wedding-transportation-ideas), consider your venue’s parking situation, guests’ access to car services or public transportation, and the cost you’re asking them to incur. A good rule of thumb: If it’s going to run them $20 or more—especially if you’ve already asked them to travel for a destination wedding—consider a shuttle bus. Some car services, such as Uber, allow you to book rides on others’ behalf.

### Book Your Transportation (Like a Limo or Specialty Car)

After you consider your guests, it’s time to think about you and your partner. Whether you want a stretch Escalade limo or a tandem bicycle, make sure to book it now.

### Book the Honeymoon

Traditionally, wedding etiquette states the groom plans a surprise honeymoon for the bride, but if you’re tag-teaming the honeymoon strategy, try to have things semi-sorted out by the five-month mark. That means being on the same page about budget, timing, travel arrangements, and a rough itinerary.

### Buy or Rent the Groom’s Tuxedo

You can opt to [buy or rent](https://www.brides.com/best-tuxedo-rentals-4780505) your suit or tuxedo. When selecting the actual ensemble, focus on fit and function. A well-made outfit will be flattering, but it should also allow you to move freely.

### Begin Premarital Counseling

Many couples attribute the success of their relationship to [premarital counseling](https://www.brides.com/story/top-premarital-counselor-questions). An objective third party can help you address issues that emerge in your dynamic—and provide counselors healthy conflict-resolution tactics, so you’ll be ready when an inevitable disagreement does present itself.

Some states offer a discount on [your marriage license](https://www.brides.com/story/who-needs-to-sign-marriage-license) if you undergo counseling.

## 4 Months Out

### Have Your Final Tasting With the Caterer

After numerous conversations with your caterer, it’s time to taste the proposed menu. The tasting has become increasingly important as more and more couples choose to customize everythin—from [their signature cocktails](https://www.brides.com/wedding-signature-cocktails-8760512) to their desserts. Consider bringing your planner to the meeting; they’ve likely attended dozens of tastings and will be your clear-eyed troubleshooter, paying attention to the detailing of the food and the attentiveness of the service.

### Choose Your Cake

If you decide to [have a wedding cake](https://www.brides.com/gallery/wedding-etiquette-tips-for-brides-wedding-cake-etiquette), this is the time to settle on a look and flavor profile. Instead of stressing out about pleasing every one of your guests, focus on the confection that would make you happy. When you know what you want, find a reputable baker who’s available on your date, and happy to take on your dream design at the right price point.

### Buy Wedding Bands

Even though you received your engagement ring months ago, it’s time to shop for your and your partner’s [wedding bands](https://www.brides.com/wedding-bands-guide-5070274). Make sure to also purchase insurance for your new valuables.

### Select the Groomsmen Attire and Schedule Fittings Within the Month

If you’re [having groomsmen](https://www.brides.com/groomsmen-attire-5025176) at your ceremony, this is the time to ensure they have their ensembles prepared. Send them a link on what to order—or make sure they know your preferred color scheme before they purchase an outfit.

### Have Your Hair and Makeup Trial

Before heading to [your hair and makeup trial](https://www.brides.com/story/when-to-have-wedding-hair-and-makeup-trials), look back at old photos of yourself or social media posts of others for inspiration. Bring the pictures with you—and be as specific as possible with the stylist about what you do and don’t want.

## 3 Months Out

### Order the Invitations and Hire a Calligrapher

There are a few [ground rules](https://www.brides.com/story/when-to-send-every-wedding-related-card-and-invitation) when it comes to ordering wedding invitations: Order enough of them to account for some mistakes, make sure they’re able arrive in time, set up a system to record RSVP replies, and confirm all addresses and spelling. However, know that when it comes to the design and [wording](https://www.brides.com/story/guide-to-wedding-invitation-wording), the options are endless. Need a little advice to rein it all in? Remind yourself that the theme of your invites should match the vibe of the wedding and you as a couple.

### Create or Plan Your Menu

Once you’ve undergone a successful tasting, you’ll have a good sense of a caterer’s style and offerings, so you’re ready to finalize the food. Maybe you hand-selected every hors d’oeuvre, main, side, dessert, and drink. Or, perhaps you just told the chef to \”handle it\” and called it a day. Either way, now is the time to stamp your approval on a completed menu that fits your budget, taste, and timing.

### Brainstorm Guest Favors and Gift Bags

Favors and gift bags are option. However, if you want to do them, now is the time to decide what they will be. Stuck on endless options? Consider [an edible treat](https://www.brides.com/gallery/edible-wedding-favors), like bags of candy or a cookie.

### Book a Photo-Booth Rental

Photo booths have become a reception staple. If you’re hoping for something with a little more pizzazz than the standard step-and-shoot, consider [these creative alternatives](https://www.brides.com/story/alternatives-to-the-traditional-photo-booth).

### Write Your Vows

If you’ve opted to [write your own](https://www.brides.com/story/guide-to-writing-your-own-wedding-vows) promises to one another, start thinking about what those should sound like for you two as a couple, whether that be traditional and classic or modern and innovative.

### Select Readings

Bible verses are often an obvious choice here, but there are plenty of [nonreligious options](https://www.brides.com/story/nonreligious-wedding-ceremony-reading-ideas), too. If you’d prefer for designated readers to choose their own, make sure to give them as much guidance as possible.

### Meet With Your Officiant

When considering an officiant, think about availability, eligibility, fee, and fit. Can your officiant of choice lawfully, affordably, and meaningfully help you two become one? Make sure they are on the same page as you about expectations and the overall tone of the ceremony. And if you’ve recruited a recently-ordained friend or family member to head up the charge, here’s an article on [how to officiate](https://www.brides.com/story/how-to-perform-wedding-ceremony) a wedding ceremony to share with them.

### Start Crafting DIY Items If You Haven’t Already

If you have any décor projects to tackle, it’s time to start crafting. Make sure to give yourself plenty of time to allow your vision to come to life.

## 2 Months Out

### Send Out the Wedding Invitations (With RSVPs Due One Month Before the Wedding)

You already did the hard part—the selection process. Now, it’s time to [print](https://www.brides.com/gallery/diy-printable-online-wedding-invitations-downloads-how-to) and [assemble](https://www.brides.com/story/assembling-your-wedding-invitations) your invites. Be sure to include a self-addressed, pre-stamped envelope for your RSVP cards.

### Send Out Rehearsal-Dinner Invitations

If your partner and their family are handling the rehearsal dinner, make sure you give them an [accurate list](https://www.brides.com/story/who-to-invite-rehearsal-dinner-etiquette) of addresses for the invitees. You don’t want it to be an exact replica of the reception that will follow the next night, but you may also want to confirm you don’t show up to a BBQ buffet in black-tie. You can also opt to send these out with your formal invitations.

### Have Your First Wedding Dress Fitting

Your first [wedding dress fitting](https://www.brides.com/story/wedding-dress-alterations-tips) should occur two to three months after ordering your gown. Your second fitting should happen about six weeks before the big day.

### Purchase Wedding Dress Undergarments

After your first dress fitting, it’s time to purchase the necessary [undergarments](https://www.brides.com/story/how-to-buy-bridal-undergarments). It’s best to wait until this point, as your first fitting will clarify what type of underpinnings—from [shapewear](https://www.brides.com/best-shapewear-for-wedding-dresses-4796832) to lingerie—the piece will require.

### Pick Up Your Marriage License

It’s a crucial step that you don’t want to forget: getting your marriage license. Every state has different laws and requirements, so make sure to check for yours ahead of time. If you’re having a destination wedding, whether domestic or international, you’ll also need to research those paperwork requirements. Then, make sure you as a couple, your witness(es), and your officiant sign the document.

### Buy Gifts for Your Wedding Party

How much you spend on [gifts for your wedding party](https://www.brides.com/editors-picks-wedding-party-gifts-july-2024-8677438) is ultimately up to you. However, no matter the price point, focus on gifting something thoughtful, functional, and personalized.

### Do a Floral Mock-Up With Your Florist

Floral samples vary depending on the florist and your décor choices. However, typically, they’ll include a mock reception table setup, centerpiece, and bouquet. Make sure to flag any necessary tweaks and finalize your delivery and care strategy.

### Give the Song Selections to Your Musicians

Now is the time to tell your band, DJ, or musicians what you want to hear at your wedding. If you need suggestions, start by considering the [most popular wedding songs of all time](https://www.brides.com/most-requested-wedding-songs-of-all-time-4774512), then think about tunes you and your soon-to-be spouse love.

### Buy All Necessary Small Items

There are a number of small items you’ll want to secure before your wedding weekend, including table numbers, toasting flutes, a [cake topper](https://www.brides.com/gallery/wedding-cake-toppers), a cake stand, a cake knife, the [guest book](https://www.brides.com/gallery/alternative-guest-book-ideas), a card box, ring-bearer accessories and flower-girl accessories. You also may consider purchasing pashminas, flip-flops, and/or sunglasses for guests to change into at the reception, as well as baskets to hold them. And don’t forget your signs (\”Welcome,\” \”Guest Book,\” \”Dancing Shoes,\” etc.).

## 1 Month Out

### Assemble Gift Bags

Follow the same guidelines as you did for for your DIY projects to ensure this task is fun rather than frustrating. Give yourself plenty of time to complete this to-do—and consider enlisting your friends for help.

### Pay Vendors in Full

The last situation you want to deal with right before your wedding day is a vendor chasing their payment. Avoid that by keeping careful track of when and how much you pay each vendor. If there are some vendors who must be paid on the day of your wedding, or you’re [distributing tips](https://www.brides.com/story/vendor-etiquette-feeding-tipping-tips), delegate that role to a trusted friend or relative.

### Create a Seating Chart

Creating the seating chart can feel like another daunting task. When completing this must-do, think about your venue’s [floor plan](https://www.brides.com/story/how-to-plan-your-wedding-reception-layout), whether or not you’ll have [a head table](https://www.brides.com/story/head-table-wedding-reception-seating) and who will be sitting at it, and your preferred design.

### Order or Make Escort Cards and Place Cards

While both [place cards and escort cards](https://www.brides.com/story/difference-between-place-card-escort-card) designate where each guest will be seated at a wedding, the former are more specific and formal than the latter. A place card not only directs guests to the table where they will sit during the reception, but also points them to their particular seat at the table. Whichever you choose, you’ll want the cards to complement your overall wedding theme.

### Have a Final Venue Walk-Through

Make a list of questions beforehand, and take your planner or another close friend or family member to bring up anything you may forget.

### Put Cash in Tip Envelopes for Your Planner/Delegate to Distribute

While you don’t [need to tip people](https://www.brides.com/story/complete-list-wedding-vendors-gratuity-tip-how-much) who own their own businesses, such as photographers, videographers, and florists, it’s typically customary to tip some vendors, including musicians, DJs, hair stylists, makeup artists, drivers, bartenders, and servers. Some couples also opt to tip their wedding planner.

### Break in Your Wedding Shoes

Strut down your hallway. Dance in the kitchen. Do everything in your power to avoid painful blisters on your wedding night.

## Final Week

Congratulations! You’ve made it all the way to the final week of wedding planning. Deep breaths now, most of the hard work is over at this point. Now’s the time to take care of the little things like:

- Manicure/pedicure
- Getting a massage
- Final dress fitting
- [Pack your bags](https://www.brides.com/honeymoon-packing-list-4843722) for the honeymoon (if you’re leaving after your wedding)
- [Clean your ring](https://www.brides.com/story/how-to-clean-engagement-ring)
- Chase any [RSVP stragglers](https://www.brides.com/story/follow-up-with-guests-who-have-not-rsvp) and deliver the final headcount
- Clear your work to-do list so you can only focus on wedding festivities and take it all in
- Practice your vows out loud
- Write your partner [a note](https://www.brides.com/writing-note-to-groom-on-wedding-day-4703028)

## Night Before and Morning of the Wedding

The big day is finally here. All that careful preparation and creative planning have come to fruition, and it’s time to enjoy the wedding. [Here’s what to do](https://www.brides.com/story/what-to-do-the-night-before-your-wedding-day):

### The Night Before:

- Eat a healthy meal
- Pack a clutch or small bag of personal items
- Drink water
- Get a good night’s sleep
- Put any boxes, suitcases, bags, and survival kits to bring to the ceremony or reception in the car

### The Morning Of:

- Stay off your feet as much as possible
- Eat breakfast
- Drink even more water
- Take your dress and veil out of the bag early on and have someone steam them if needed
- Lay out all the items (rings, invitations, etc.) that you want the photographer to capture
- Exchange notes with your partner
- [Say thank you](https://www.brides.com/bridesmaid-thank-you-card-5092968) to everyone around you
